sections.heading: The idea
sections.body_md:
An overdetermined linear equation \(Ax \approx b\) usually has no exact solution. Least squares asks for the \(x\) that makes the residual \(Ax - b\) as small as possible in the Euclidean norm. When the columns of \(A\) are independent, that \(x\) is the solution of the normal equations \(A^T A x = A^T b\). The same equation says the residual is orthogonal to every column of \(A\). Geometrically, \(Ax\) is the orthogonal projection of \(b\) onto the column space.

The Gram matrix \(A^T A\) is invertible exactly when the columns are independent, and then the minimizer is unique. If the columns are dependent, the normal equations stay consistent but the minimizer is not unique. Setting a gradient of the squared residual to zero is how those equations are derived. That derivation, and the pseudoinverse that writes the same minimizer, is a later skill. This skill is the equation and the rank condition.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
The normal equations and the full-column-rank solution are
\[
A^T A x = A^T b, \qquad x = (A^T A)^{-1} A^T b.
\]
For one column \((p, q)\) and a right-hand side \((u, v)\), the scalar unknown is \((p u + q v)/(p^2 + q^2)\). The residual of the fitted vector is orthogonal to the columns.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
Four measurements of one unknown are \(1, 9, 3, 11\), and the column is a column of ones. The normal equation is \(4x = 24\).

The gauge mean is 6. The residual is \((-5, 3, -3, 5)\), and it sums to zero, which is orthogonality against the single column of ones. The squared residual is \(25 + 9 + 9 + 25 = 68\). The fit is unique because a nonzero column has full column rank. It is not an exact fit, and least squares does not pretend that it is.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: Replacing \(A^T b\) by \(b\) is the algebra error that breaks the shapes. The right-hand side has to live in the column space of \(A^T\). A second error is to declare \(A^T A\) invertible just because \(A\) is tall. Tall matrices can have repeated columns. A third is to use the full-row-rank formula \((AA^T)^{-1}\) on a tall full-column-rank matrix. That Gram matrix is the large one, and it is singular. A fourth is to expect a zero residual. A zero residual means \(b\) was already in the column space. The normal equations do not require that.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: Fitting a model that is linear in its parameters uses these normal equations with columns built from the data. Reading a gain and a time constant from step and frequency records is system identification, and the scalar fit \(y = \theta u\) is the same equation. Deriving the normal equations as the stationarity condition of a quadratic, and writing the minimizer as a pseudoinverse, is the next skill.
